title: Social Media Self-Presentation
hook: A profile photo is body language frozen and multiplied, read by strangers in a fraction of a second and remembered long after you have changed.
why:
For many people, the first time someone sees them is no longer in person. A recruiter looks at a profile on a professional network, a potential date scrolls past a picture on an app, a new colleague looks you up before a meeting, a client checks your photo on a company website. In each case, a single still image is doing the work that a handshake, a voice and a few minutes of conversation used to do.

That image is body language: a face, an expression, a posture, an angle, a setting. But it is body language with unusual properties. It is chosen rather than spontaneous. It is seen by many more people than any real encounter. It is judged in a fraction of a second, without the correction that a conversation would bring. And it lasts, sometimes for years after the person in it has changed. This chapter looks at how quickly faces in photos are judged, how much those judgments matter, how much photos of the same person vary, why other people choose better photos of you than you do, what the feed does to men's sense of their own bodies, how to read other people's curated selves, and how to present yourself honestly. It is the mirror image of the rest of this part: instead of reading others, it is about how you are read when you are not there.

teach.p:
In 2006 Janine Willis and Alexander Todorov showed people photographs of unfamiliar faces for different lengths of time, from a tenth of a second to a full second, and asked them to judge traits such as trustworthiness, competence, likeability, aggressiveness and attractiveness. They compared these quick judgments with judgments made by other people who could look at the same faces for as long as they liked.

The judgments made after a tenth of a second were already closely in line with the untimed ones. Trustworthiness showed the strongest agreement. Giving people more time made little difference to what they concluded. It did make them more confident in their judgments, and slightly more negative.

This does not mean the judgments were accurate. The study measured agreement between viewers, not whether the faces belonged to people who were really trustworthy or competent. Part I's chapter on the face discussed how weak the link between facial appearance and character tends to be. What the study shows is that people form a firm impression of a face almost instantly, and that looking longer mainly increases their confidence in it.

For a profile photo, this has a plain implication. Most people who see it will look for well under a second, scrolling past in a list of other faces. In that moment they will form an impression of whether you seem trustworthy, warm and capable, and they will feel sure of it. The figure here is seen at three quarters, the angle of a typical portrait. A viewer has already decided something about him.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if impressions formed after a tenth of a second differed substantially from those formed without a time limit. Willis and Todorov found they were closely in line, with more time adding confidence rather than changing the judgment.

teach.p:
Snap judgments from faces are not only formed quickly. They can shape real decisions. In 2005 Alexander Todorov and his colleagues showed people pairs of photographs of the winner and runner-up in elections for the United States Senate and House of Representatives, without telling them who the candidates were. Participants were asked which candidate looked more competent, often after seeing the faces for about a second.

The candidate judged more competent from his face had won roughly seven times out of ten Senate races. Judgments of other traits, such as how attractive or likeable a candidate looked, did not predict the results. Only the impression of competence did. The participants knew nothing about the candidates' records or policies. They were responding to faces alone.

Later work has found similar effects in other countries, though with variation. None of this means that voters choose only on faces. It means that the impression a face makes is one influence among many, and that it can be strong enough to matter when other information is weak or the contest is close.

If the faces of experienced politicians can sway elections, the faces in profile photos can certainly sway the smaller decisions made about ordinary people: whom to interview, whom to message, whom to trust with a contract. These impressions are formed from a single image in a single second, and they have little to do with the person's actual competence. The figure here stands upright with hands behind his back, the formal bearing of an official portrait, a pose chosen precisely because of how it is read.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if competence judgments from candidates' faces bore no relation to election outcomes. Todorov and colleagues found they predicted the winner in roughly seven out of ten Senate races, though other factors also mattered.
teach.pullQuote: A face is judged in a fraction of a second, and looking longer mostly makes people more sure of what they already concluded.

teach.p:
It is natural to think of a face as fixed, so that any reasonable photo of you shows more or less the same person. Research on face recognition shows otherwise. In 2011 Rob Jenkins, David White, Xandra van Montfort and Mike Burton collected many everyday photographs of the same individuals, the kind of images found online, and asked people who did not know them to sort the photos by identity.

People who were unfamiliar with the faces greatly overestimated how many different people were in the set, treating photos of the same person as photos of different people. People who knew the individuals sorted them easily. The researchers also found that ratings of attractiveness varied more between different photos of the same person than between different people. Lighting, angle, expression, camera distance and the moment of capture changed faces far more than viewers realised.

Todorov and his colleagues later showed the same thing for impressions of character: different photos of one person can produce quite different judgments of trustworthiness or competence. A face is not one image. It is a range of images, and any single photo samples one point in that range.

This is good news for anyone choosing a profile photo, because it means the photo matters and can be chosen well. It is also a caution for anyone judging others from a photo. The image you are reacting to may be an unlucky moment, a bad angle or an old picture, and the person may look and seem quite different in life. The figure here tilts his head slightly, a small change that alters how a whole face is read.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if different photos of the same person produced consistent impressions. Jenkins and colleagues found that attractiveness varied more across photos of one person than between people, and later work found the same for impressions of character.

teach.p:
If photos vary so much, the obvious step is to choose the best one. The difficulty is that people are not very good at choosing photos of themselves. In 2017 David White, Clare Sutherland and Amy Burton asked people to choose, from a set of their own photographs, the ones they would use for a social media profile, a dating site or a professional network. They also had strangers choose from the same photos. Then other strangers rated the chosen images.

Photos chosen by strangers made better impressions than photos people chose for themselves. The researchers called it the curse of self. When we look at our own photos, we see them through our own feelings about our faces: the feature we dislike, the expression we remember feeling awkward about, the way we think we look. Strangers see what other strangers will see.

This suggests a simple practice. Collect a dozen recent, natural photos of yourself, and ask several people who do not know you well, or who can be frank, to choose the ones that make the best impression for the purpose you have in mind. A professional network, a dating app and a company website may need different choices. Natural expressions tend to work better than posed ones, and a genuine smile, as the chapter on the poker face earlier in this part described, generally helps more than it costs.

It is also worth matching the photo to the setting. A photo taken at a wedding may show you happy and at ease, but cropped onto a professional profile it can look out of place. The figure here stands with weight on one hip, relaxed and at ease, the kind of unguarded posture that a friend's camera often catches and that the person in the picture might never have chosen.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if people chose photos of themselves that made better impressions than those chosen by strangers. White, Sutherland and Burton found the reverse.

teach.p:
Social media does not only show others your body. It shows you everyone else's. For men, much of what is shown is a narrow ideal: lean, muscular, often shirtless, photographed in flattering light after a workout, sometimes edited, occasionally enhanced with drugs. Fitness influencers, celebrity transformations and advertising present this body as normal and achievable.

Experiments have found that it affects men who see it. In one 2020 study, Marika Tiggemann and Isabella Anderberg showed young men Instagram images of muscular, bare-chested men, of the same men clothed, or of scenery. Those who saw the bare-chested images were less satisfied with their own bodies afterwards. Other studies have found similar short-term effects, though the size varies and not every study finds them. Surveys link heavy use of appearance-focused social media with concern about muscularity, though they cannot show which comes first.

Part II's chapters dealt with what the body shows when a person is struggling. Here the point is narrower: what you scroll through shapes how you feel about your own body, and therefore how you hold it. A man who has spent half an hour comparing himself with fitness accounts may stand and move differently from one who has not, more self-conscious and less at ease.

The practical steps are simple, if not easy. Notice how you feel after time on particular accounts. Unfollow those that leave you feeling worse. Remember that many such images are the best of hundreds of attempts, taken in ideal conditions. And spend time in places where real bodies are visible, from the gym changing room to the beach, where the range of normal is far wider than any feed suggests. The figure here stands slumped, the posture that can follow a long session of comparison.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if men's body satisfaction were unaffected by viewing idealised muscular images. Tiggemann and Anderberg found it fell after such images, though effects vary across studies and most measure only the short term.

teach.p:
Every feed is a selection. People post their holidays, promotions, new babies and best photos, and rarely their arguments, rejections, bad days or sleepless nights. Readers know this in principle. In practice, the steady stream of good news shapes their sense of how other people's lives are going.

In 2011 Alexander Jordan, Benoît Monin, Carol Dweck and their colleagues found that people consistently underestimate how often others experience negative emotions, while estimating positive emotions more accurately. Part of the reason was that people tend to hide their negative feelings and show their positive ones, so others see a skewed sample. People who underestimated others' negative experiences more tended to report lower satisfaction with their own lives. The study was not about social media, which magnifies the same skew.

The lesson for reading others is to treat a feed as a highlight reel, not as evidence of how someone is. A friend whose posts are cheerful may be struggling. A colleague whose life looks effortless online may be finding things as hard as you are. You cannot read a person's state from what they choose to post, any more than you could read a man's mood from his best suit.

Changes can be worth noticing, with care. A friend who usually posts often and suddenly goes silent, or whose posts change markedly in tone, may simply be busy or taking a break. It may also be worth a message, in the spirit of the chapters in Part II and Part III on checking in: not a diagnosis, just a question. The figure here slouches low on a sofa, phone in hand, comparing his ordinary evening with everyone else's best moments.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if people estimated others' negative emotions as accurately as their positive ones. Jordan and colleagues found people consistently underestimated how often others felt bad, partly because negative feelings are hidden more often.

teach.p:
If impressions from photos are fast, strong and variable, there is a temptation to manage them hard: heavy filters, flattering angles, carefully staged settings, a body that has been edited. Some curation is normal and harmless. Everyone chooses a decent photo rather than an unflattering one. But there are good reasons to keep self-presentation honest.

The first is practical. A photo that does not look like you on a good day creates an expectation that the first meeting cannot meet. On dating apps, this is a familiar source of disappointment. At work, a profile picture that is ten years old makes the first video call slightly awkward. The best photo is one that looks like you as people will meet you.

The second is about the people around you. Your photos often include others, and posting an image of a friend, a colleague or a child shapes how they are seen by people they have never met. Asking before you post, especially for images of children or of people in vulnerable moments, extends to others the care you would want for yourself.

The third is permanence. A post can be found years later by an employer, a partner or a child, and the person you were when you posted it may not be the person you are. It is worth asking, before posting, whether you would be content for this image to represent you in five years. Presence online, like presence in a room, works best when it is congruent: when the image, the words and the person all match. The figure here stands open and at ease, as he might look to anyone who met him in person.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if heavily edited or outdated photos made first meetings go as smoothly as accurate ones. The mismatch between image and person is a common source of disappointment, though this is drawn more from experience than from controlled studies.
teach.pullQuote: The best photo is one that looks like you as people will meet you.

poseGallery.annotation: A tough, posed shot may look confident to you and cold to strangers. A relaxed, natural image usually reads as warmer and just as capable.

caseStudy:
Callum, thirty-one, was looking for a new job and, after a breakup, had started using a dating app. On both, he used photos he had chosen himself: a serious headshot with his arms folded for the professional network, and for the app a gym selfie taken after months of training, along with a photo from a stag weekend. He had few responses on either.

A friend who worked in recruitment offered to look. She said the headshot made him look severe, and that the gym selfie said more about the gym than about him. She went through his phone and picked out three photos he had never considered: one of him laughing at a barbecue, one of him talking to someone at a friend's wedding, and a plain, smiling photo his sister had taken on a walk.

He was sceptical. He thought he looked tired in one and that his smile was lopsided in another. But he used them. Within a fortnight, two recruiters had contacted him, and conversations on the dating app began to go further. Several people mentioned that he looked friendly.

Around the same time, he noticed that he felt worse about himself on days when he spent time on fitness accounts, and that he had been comparing his body with men who trained for a living. He unfollowed most of them. He kept training, but stopped photographing it. When he met someone from the app for the first time, she said he looked exactly like his pictures, which he decided was the best review a profile could get.
observe: Notice how quickly you form an impression of someone from a profile photo, and how sure of it you feel.
Notice how different you look across several photos taken of you in the same month.
Notice how you feel about your own body after time on particular accounts or feeds.
Notice a friend whose feed looks effortless, and whether you know how they are actually doing.

drills.name: Stranger's Choice
steps: Collect twelve recent, natural photos of yourself, including some you would not choose.
Decide what the photo is for: a professional profile, a dating app or a company page.
Ask three people who do not know you well, or who will be frank, to choose their top two for that purpose.
Compare their choices with your own.
Try one of their choices for a month.

drills.name: Feed Audit
steps: Scroll through the accounts you follow for five minutes, noticing how you feel about your body and your life.
List any accounts that reliably leave you feeling worse.
Unfollow or mute at least two of them.
After a week, notice whether anything has changed.

drills.name: Behind the Highlights
steps: Choose three friends whose feeds look as if things are going well.
Write down what you actually know about how each is doing, apart from their posts.
Send one of them a message asking how they are, without referring to their posts.

drills.name: Five-Year Test
steps: Before posting anything about yourself or others this week, pause.
Ask whether you would be content for it to represent you in five years.
If it includes someone else, ask whether they would be content too, or ask them.
Note how often the pause changed what you posted.

quiz.q: A friend says he can judge people from profile photos better if he looks at them carefully for a while. What did Willis and Todorov find?
options: Longer viewing made judgments far more accurate, so careful study of a photo pays off
Judgments after a tenth of a second matched untimed ones; more time mainly added confidence
Judgments after a tenth of a second were random and bore no relation to longer ones
Longer viewing made people less confident, because they noticed more contradictory details
quiz.explain: Impressions formed in a tenth of a second were closely in line with untimed ones. More time increased confidence rather than changing the judgment, and the study did not show the judgments were accurate.

quiz.q: In Todorov and colleagues' 2005 study, which judgment from candidates' faces predicted election results?
options: How attractive the candidates looked to the participants
How likeable and friendly the candidates appeared to be
How competent the candidates looked, often after a second
How old the candidates appeared, relative to their rivals
quiz.explain: The candidate judged more competent from his face had won roughly seven of ten Senate races. Judgments of attractiveness and likeability did not predict the results.

quiz.q: What did Jenkins and colleagues find when people sorted everyday photos of unfamiliar faces?
options: They sorted them accurately, because a face looks much the same in every photo
They sorted them accurately when the photos had all been taken by professional photographers
They grouped photos of different people together, because all the faces looked alike
They treated photos of one person as different people, and attractiveness varied widely
quiz.explain: Unfamiliar viewers greatly overestimated the number of people in the set, and attractiveness varied more across photos of one person than between people. Any single photo samples one point in a wide range.

quiz.q: According to White, Sutherland and Burton, who chooses profile photos that make the best impression?
options: Strangers choosing from your photos, rather than you choosing for yourself
You, because you know which photos look most like you in your everyday life
Close family, because they know you best and see you most kindly
A professional photographer, choosing from a studio session alone
quiz.explain: Photos chosen by strangers made better impressions than those people chose for themselves. The researchers called it the curse of self: we see our own photos through our feelings about our faces.

quiz.q: A friend's posts show a promotion, a holiday and a new flat, and you feel your own life is falling behind. What does Jordan and colleagues' research suggest?
options: Your friend's life is probably going as well as the posts suggest, so your feeling is accurate
People underestimate how often others feel bad, partly because negative feelings are hidden
People overestimate others' negative feelings, so your friend is probably even happier
Comparing yourself with others is harmless, because people know that posts are selective
quiz.explain: People consistently underestimate others' negative experiences, partly because those are hidden more than positive ones. A feed magnifies that skew, so it is poor evidence of how someone is really doing.

quiz.q: You need a new photo for a professional profile. Which approach fits this chapter best?
options: Ask a few frank people to choose from several recent, natural photos for that purpose
Use the photo you like best of yourself, since you know your own face better than others
Use a heavily edited photo, since first impressions from photos are formed so very fast
Use an old photo from your best year, since impressions do not change much over time
quiz.explain: Others choose better photos of us than we do, and photos vary widely. A recent, natural photo also matches how people will meet you, which avoids a mismatch later.

reflection.prompt: Look at one specific profile photo you currently use, on any platform. Describe it as a stranger would: your expression, posture, angle, clothing and setting. What impression do you think it gives in the first second? Who chose it, and why? Then think about the accounts you follow, and describe how you usually feel about your own body and life after scrolling through them. What one change would you make to how you present yourself or what you look at?
reflection.guidance: Most people find it hard to see their own photos as strangers do, which is exactly the point of the curse of self. Be specific about what is in the image rather than how you feel about it. If you can, ask someone else to describe it too, and compare their description with yours.

failureMode: The first failure is to believe that people will look at your photo carefully, when most will judge it in a fraction of a second and feel sure of their judgment. The second is to choose your own photos and trust your own preferences, when strangers reliably choose better. The third is to judge others confidently from a single image, when photos of the same person vary more than photos of different people. The fourth is to let a feed of idealised male bodies set your sense of what is normal, and to carry that comparison into how you hold yourself. The fifth is to read others' curated highlights as evidence of their real lives. And the sixth is to present an image so edited or out of date that the person who arrives cannot match it.
